reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by activating germline variants in the MET proto-oncogene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, and one of the few kidney cancer syndromes driven by an oncogene rather than a tumour suppressor
Characterised by multiple, bilateral type 1 papillary renal cell carcinomas that are typically low-grade but numerous
Tumours often accumulate slowly, allowing nephron-sparing strategies, and management commonly follows a size-threshold approach to intervention to preserve renal function
Unlike some other renal cancer syndromes it lacks prominent extrarenal manifestations, so isolated multifocal papillary tumours should prompt consideration of the diagnosis
The causative MET mutations frequently involve the tyrosine kinase domain and may be reinforced by non-random duplication of the mutant-bearing chromosome
MET-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors are relevant options for advanced or unresectable disease
Surveillance relies on periodic cross-sectional renal imaging to detect and monitor new tumours
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome is driven by germline gain-of-function variants in MET, which encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase for hepatocyte growth factor. Mutations in the kinase domain cause constitutive, ligand-independent receptor activation, switching on downstream proliferation and survival signalling in renal tubular cells. This oncogenic drive, often amplified by duplication of the chromosome carrying the mutant allele, promotes the development of the characteristic multiple bilateral type 1 papillary renal cell carcinomas.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (FH)
Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal involvement
Sporadic multifocal papillary renal cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Germline MET sequencing and analysis for kinase-domain variants
Periodic cross-sectional renal imaging with CT or MRI
Histopathological confirmation of type 1 papillary renal cell carcinoma
Assessment of renal function to guide nephron-sparing management
Tumour molecular testing to inform MET-targeted therapy in advanced disease
Family history review and consideration of imaging in at-risk relatives
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging renal mass or one exceeding the intervention threshold
Haematuria, flank pain or a palpable mass suggesting advanced tumour
Radiological features atypical for indolent type 1 papillary disease
reference.prognosis: Tumours are usually low-grade and slow-growing, so with imaging surveillance and timely nephron-sparing surgery renal function can be preserved and outcomes are generally good. Prognosis worsens with high-grade or metastatic disease, where MET-directed systemic therapy becomes relevant.
pitfalls: Recommending radical nephrectomy when nephron-sparing surgery would preserve function in this multifocal, bilateral disease
Overlooking a germline cause in a patient with multiple papillary renal tumours
Intervening on small stable lesions rather than following an appropriate size threshold
Failing to offer genetic evaluation and imaging to at-risk relatives
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Kidney Cancer and Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment
management: For localized, multifocal small renal masses (the typical presentation), use a surveillance and treat strategy, imaging each tumor at intervals and reserving surgery for lesions that grow to a threshold size or show suspicious change rather than treating every lesion.

Nephron sparing partial nephrectomy is preferred whenever technically feasible, since multifocal or familial RCC is a recognized indication favoring partial over radical nephrectomy and helps preserve renal function across a lifetime of recurring tumors.

Thermal ablation (cryoablation or radiofrequency ablation) is a reasonable kidney sparing alternative for small tumors, particularly for repeat, low volume disease where preserving nephrons matters most, accepting a somewhat higher local recurrence rate than surgery.

Radical nephrectomy is reserved for tumors not amenable to nephron sparing surgery; pre-surgical tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy has in some cases been used to downstage a tumor so a nephron sparing operation becomes possible.
Lymphadenectomy is not routinely required for clinically localized disease.

For advanced, unresectable, or metastatic disease, MET directed therapy (such as foretinib) has shown activity in papillary RCC including HPRC with germline MET mutation, with the strongest responses in patients carrying germline MET mutations; this is supportive evidence for MET-directed therapy in this population, not an established or preferred regimen.

VEGF-pathway tyrosine kinase inhibitors and mTOR pathway inhibitors can be considered as systemic options for advanced non-clear-cell (including papillary) RCC, with mTOR inhibitors generally reserved for later lines behind newer agents.

Choice of specific systemic agent, immune checkpoint inhibitor, or MET inhibitor for advanced disease should follow current NCCN kidney cancer guidance, and clinical trial enrollment should be pursued where feasible given the rarity of the disease.
Routine adjuvant systemic therapy after resection is not currently supported for this histology and should not be presented as standard management.
Radiotherapy has no defined curative role; it may be considered for palliation of symptomatic, unresectable disease with major venous (IVC) involvement.

Monitor with risk-stratified surveillance combining history and physical exam, laboratory testing, and cross-sectional abdominal imaging plus chest imaging, at intervals that intensify with higher clinicopathologic risk.

Because new tumors can arise throughout life in both kidneys, lifelong periodic renal imaging is appropriate rather than time-limited post-treatment surveillance alone, tracking each lesion against an intervention threshold and monitoring renal function to guide how aggressively new lesions are treated.

Refer patients and at-risk relatives to urologic oncology with expertise in nephron-sparing surgery for hereditary kidney cancer syndromes, and to clinical genetics for germline MET testing, inheritance counseling, and risk-based imaging of relatives.

Refer to medical oncology once disease becomes unresectable, high grade, or metastatic, ideally with consideration of clinical trial enrollment given the rarity of the disease and limited direct evidence for systemic therapy in HPRC specifically.
